Atomicity & messaging::Locks and leases.summary: Use SET with NX and a bounded PX lifetime to claim a resource, storing a unique token as proof of ownership. Release only after atomically confirming that the key still contains that token.
Atomicity & messaging::Locks and leases.explanation: A lock is a Redis key created conditionally with SET NX and a bounded PX lifetime. Store a value unique to the acquiring request, and release the key only after atomically verifying that the stored value still matches that token; otherwise an expired lease might have been acquired by another worker while the original work was still finishing.

parameters.name: resource_name
parameters.description: The lock key identifying the shared resource.

parameters.name: my_random_value
parameters.description: A value unique across clients and lock requests, used as the ownership token.

parameters.name: NX
parameters.description: Only set when the key does not already exist.
Expiration duration in milliseconds.

Atomicity & messaging::Locks and leases.returns: SET returns success when the lease is acquired; otherwise acquisition fails. The ownership-check release returns deletion only when the stored value matches the caller's token.

example.title: Token-checked Redis lease
example.explanation: Creates a 30-second lease using a unique token and removes it only when the stored token still belongs to this worker.

useCases.title: Exclusive resource processing
useCases.scenario: Several workers may process the same resource concurrently.

useCases.title: Crash recovery through expiry
useCases.scenario: A worker can crash or lose connectivity while holding a lock.

useCases.title: Majority-based Redlock acquisition
useCases.scenario: A lock must coordinate clients across multiple independent Redis instances.

interview.question: How do you acquire a Redis lock safely?
interview.answer: Use SET with NX so only a request that finds the key absent creates it, and PX to attach a finite lifetime. The stored value should be unique to the client and request.
interview.followUp: Why is a finite lifetime necessary? It ensures a failed client does not retain the resource forever; the remaining validity must also account for acquisition time.

interview.question: Why must lock release verify a token?
interview.answer: Release it with an atomic check that compares the key’s current value with the caller’s token, deleting only on equality. A plain DEL could remove a newer owner’s lock after the original lease expired.
interview.followUp: What can happen if the lease expires during work? A different client may acquire the key, so the old worker must not perform ownership-sensitive cleanup or assume exclusivity.

interview.question: How does Redlock differ from a single Redis lock?
interview.answer: The basic single-instance pattern uses one Redis key with a TTL. Redlock extends acquisition across multiple independent instances and accepts the lock only when a majority succeeds before the validity period runs out.
interview.followUp: How is remaining validity calculated? Start with the configured validity and subtract the elapsed time spent acquiring the lock.

keyPoints: Acquire a bounded lease with SET, a unique value, NX, and a millisecond expiration.
NX makes acquisition conditional, preventing competing requests from overwriting an existing owner.
Treat the value as an ownership token generated for each acquisition attempt.
Release requires an atomic value comparison followed by deletion.
In Redlock, subtract acquisition latency from the original lease duration before using the lock.
gotchas: A lease can expire before the protected work ends, so the worker must not assume ownership remains valid for the whole operation.
Never use a shared constant token: another request could present the same value and incorrectly pass the ownership check.
For the multi-instance Redlock algorithm, acquisition also depends on reaching a majority within the validity window.

Atomicity & messaging::Lua scripts and f.summary: Redis Lua scripts execute bounded application logic inside the server, letting related reads and writes happen atomically with fewer client round trips. Because execution blocks Redis, scripts should be short and predictable.
Atomicity & messaging::Lua scripts and f.explanation: Lua scripts run inside Redis and can combine reads, condition checks, and writes into one atomic operation. Redis executes the whole script synchronously, so clients cannot observe an intermediate state; keep the work bounded because the server is blocked for the script's entire runtime.

parameters.name: script
parameters.description: Lua source code to execute.

parameters.name: numkeys
parameters.description: Number of key names that follow the script.

parameters.name: keys
parameters.description: Key names referenced by the script through KEYS.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Additional values referenced by the script through ARGV.

Atomicity & messaging::Lua scripts and f.returns: The script's return value, produced by its final Lua expression or return statement and encoded as a Redis reply.

example.title: Atomic conditional write
example.code:
local current = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
if not current then
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
  return 1
end
return 0
example.explanation: Run with EVAL, passing one key and the value to set. The read and conditional write execute together on Redis.

useCases.scenario: A value should be checked and updated without another client changing it between operations.

useCases.title: Multi-key coordination

useCases.title: Round-trip reduction
useCases.scenario: Client-side branching would require several network round trips.

interview.question: What does atomic execution mean for a Redis Lua script?
interview.answer: Redis runs a Lua script atomically: its effects are applied as one indivisible operation, and clients cannot observe an intermediate state. The script executes on the server through Redis's embedded Lua 5.1 interpreter.
interview.followUp: What is the availability trade-off? The script blocks all server activity for its complete runtime, so logic should remain short and bounded.

interview.question: How are inputs passed to a Lua script?
interview.answer: Use EVAL with the script source, the number of keys, then the key arguments and other arguments. Inside Lua, access keys through KEYS and non-key values through ARGV.
interview.followUp: Why distinguish KEYS from ARGV? Redis uses the explicit key list to identify the keys the script operates on, while other inputs belong in ARGV.

interview.question: How does Lua invoke Redis commands?
interview.answer: redis.call() invokes a Redis command and returns its reply, while redis.pcall() provides protected-call behavior for command errors. Both are available to server-side Lua code.
interview.followUp: When is pcall useful? Use it when the script needs to handle a Redis-command error rather than aborting immediately.

keyPoints: Server-side Lua moves multi-step application logic next to the data, reducing client round trips.
EVAL sends and executes a Lua script directly on Redis.
A script can coordinate conditional changes across multiple keys and data types as one operation.
Use redis.call for normal command execution or redis.pcall when protected error handling is needed.
SCRIPT LOAD caches source by digest so later invocations can use the cached script path.
gotchas: A script blocks every connected client while it runs, so avoid expensive or unbounded computation.
The blocking behavior is global, not limited to clients that invoked the script.

Atomicity & messaging::MULTI, EXEC and W.summary: Redis MULTI queues commands and EXEC runs them sequentially as an atomic group. WATCH adds optimistic concurrency control: if a watched key changes before EXEC, Redis aborts the transaction and the client can retry.
Atomicity & messaging::MULTI, EXEC and W.explanation: MULTI starts a transaction and queues subsequent commands rather than running them immediately. EXEC runs the queued commands sequentially as one uninterrupted group; WATCH adds an optimistic check, causing EXEC to abort when a watched key changed before commit, so the application can retry with fresh data.
Atomicity & messaging::MULTI, EXEC and W.returns: MULTI returns OK; EXEC returns the transaction's command results, or a Null reply when a watched key changed.

example.title: Optimistic update with WATCH and MULTI
example.explanation: Reads a value, watches it, and commits related updates only if the watched key remains unchanged.

useCases.title: Optimistic compare-and-set
useCases.scenario: Update a value only when it is still the version or balance previously read.

useCases.title: Atomic grouped updates
useCases.scenario: Apply several related writes without another client interleaving commands between them.

useCases.title: Conflict-aware cache coordination
useCases.scenario: Retry a cache mutation after another worker changes the same key during preparation.

interview.question: What do MULTI and EXEC guarantee?
interview.answer: MULTI switches the connection into transaction mode and queues later commands. EXEC then executes the queued commands sequentially, without another client request being served between commands.
interview.followUp: Can commands from another client interleave inside the transaction? No: Redis serializes the transaction's queued commands as one uninterrupted execution.

interview.question: How does WATCH prevent stale updates?
interview.answer: WATCH provides check-and-set behavior by monitoring selected keys. If any watched key changes before EXEC, EXEC returns a null reply and the queued transaction does not run.
interview.followUp: Does WATCH block competing clients? No: it is optimistic; competing work proceeds, and the transaction is rejected if the watched state changes.

interview.question: How should an application respond to a concurrent modification?
interview.answer: Use WATCH before reading the values used to calculate an update, then start MULTI, queue the writes, and call EXEC. A null result indicates a conflict, so reread current values and retry.
interview.followUp: What should happen after a conflict? Retry the read-and-commit sequence using fresh data, with an application-level limit or failure policy.

keyPoints: A transaction groups several Redis commands into one commit attempt.
Queued commands run in their submitted order, producing a deterministic sequence within the transaction.
Other clients cannot interleave requests while the transaction executes.
After MULTI, commands are deferred until EXEC rather than taking effect immediately.
WATCH enables optimistic compare-before-commit behavior for transaction inputs.
Clients can detect a concurrent modification by checking for a null EXEC result.
gotchas: A watched-key change makes the entire transaction fail; handle EXEC returning a null reply and retry or report a conflict.
Do not assume only another client can invalidate WATCH: local writes, expiration, and eviction can also cause aborts.

Atomicity & messaging::Pipelining.summary: Redis pipelining batches independent commands so a client can send them without waiting for each reply, reducing network round trips. It improves communication efficiency but does not by itself make the batch atomic.
Atomicity & messaging::Pipelining.explanation: A pipeline queues several Redis commands so the client can send them together and read the replies in one step. This reduces request-and-response network overhead, but pipelining alone does not provide the uninterrupted execution guarantee of a transaction; use a transaction when atomic execution is required.
Atomicity & messaging::Pipelining.returns: The client receives one response for each queued command, in the same order as the commands were sent.

example.title: Batch independent commands
example.code:
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
with r.pipeline(transaction=False) as pipe:
    pipe.set("name", "Ada")
    pipe.get("name")
    results = pipe.execute()
print(results)
example.explanation: Queues independent commands, sends them together, and returns their results in command order.

useCases.title: Batch independent key operations
useCases.scenario: A service must update or read many unrelated keys during one request.

useCases.title: Reduce round trips for bulk cache work
useCases.scenario: A client performs bulk cache warming or invalidation.

useCases.title: Process commands in bounded batches
useCases.scenario: An application needs to queue many commands while controlling memory use.

interview.question: What problem does Redis pipelining solve?
interview.answer: Pipelining sends multiple commands without waiting for each individual reply, then reads the replies together. Its main benefit is reducing network and processing overhead caused by repeated request-response exchanges.
interview.followUp: Does pipelining make commands atomic? No. Use a transaction when the commands must execute in an uninterrupted sequence.

interview.question: How does a pipeline reduce latency?
interview.answer: The client writes several commands to the same connection before reading their responses. Redis processes the requests and the client later reads the responses in order.
interview.followUp: Why batch rather than pipeline indefinitely? Very large queues can increase memory use, so send a reasonable batch, read replies, and continue.

interview.question: When should a transaction be used instead?
interview.answer: Pipelining and transactions are different features. A pipeline improves communication efficiency, while a transaction provides uninterrupted execution for its commands.
interview.followUp: When are independent commands a good pipeline workload? When their correctness does not depend on isolation from other clients.

keyPoints: A client can issue multiple commands before waiting for any individual response.
Commands can be written to the server in succession, then their responses can be read afterward.
Reading replies together reduces repeated network round trips.
The technique is broadly available through Redis client libraries.
Pipelining is a long-standing Redis capability and is available across Redis versions.
gotchas: Do not create an unbounded pipeline: split large workloads into reasonably sized batches so queued commands and replies do not consume excessive memory.

Atomicity & messaging::Pub/Sub.summary: Redis Pub/Sub broadcasts channel messages to currently subscribed clients in publication order. It is at-most-once delivery: disconnected subscribers cannot replay missed messages, so use it only when loss is acceptable or separately handled.
Atomicity & messaging::Pub/Sub.explanation: A Redis client subscribes to one or more channels, while another client publishes payloads to those channels. Redis pushes each published message to clients currently subscribed to the matching channel, preserving publication order; delivery is at-most-once, so an unavailable subscriber cannot recover a missed message.
Atomicity & messaging::Pub/Sub.syntax: PUBLISH channel message; SUBSCRIBE channel [channel ...]; PSUBSCRIBE pattern [pattern ...]
Atomicity & messaging::Pub/Sub.returns: PUBLISH returns the number of clients that received the message; subscription commands emit subscription and message events rather than a durable result.

example.title: Transient cache invalidation broadcast
example.code:
redis-cli SUBSCRIBE cache:invalidate
# In another terminal:
redis-cli PUBLISH cache:invalidate '{"key":"user:42"}'
example.explanation: Run the subscriber first, then publish an invalidation event from another client. The subscriber receives the event only while its subscription is active.

useCases.title: Cache invalidation signals
useCases.scenario: A cache entry changes and active application instances should promptly discard their local copy.

useCases.title: Transient fan-out events
useCases.scenario: Connected clients need ephemeral updates such as presence or live notifications.

useCases.title: Best-effort broadcast
useCases.scenario: Multiple workers need the same noncritical notification, with missed notifications handled by a separate reconciliation path.

interview.question: What delivery guarantee does Redis Pub/Sub provide?
interview.answer: Redis Pub/Sub uses at-most-once delivery. A message reaches each client currently subscribed to its channel, but Redis does not retain it for disconnected clients or retry delivery after a failure.
interview.followUp: How would you support recovery? Use a durable Redis mechanism such as Streams, where consumers can read retained entries and acknowledge or track progress.

interview.question: How does message routing work?
interview.answer: The publisher sends a channel and payload with PUBLISH. Redis fans that payload out to all currently subscribed clients, and subscribers receive messages in publication order.
interview.followUp: What happens if there are no subscribers? The publication is not stored, so a later subscriber cannot receive it.

interview.question: How do exact and pattern subscriptions differ?
interview.answer: SUBSCRIBE registers exact channel names, while PSUBSCRIBE registers glob-style patterns. A client in subscribed mode receives matching published messages and can manage its subscriptions with the Pub/Sub commands.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does pattern subscription introduce? It is convenient for channel families, but broad patterns can deliver more traffic than narrowly selected channels.

keyPoints: Publishers name channels rather than individual recipients; subscribers independently register interest in those channels.
Within the documented Pub/Sub flow, consumers observe messages according to their publication order.
Each published message is delivered zero or one time; Pub/Sub provides no duplicate redelivery guarantee.
After Redis sends a message, the Pub/Sub system does not offer a second delivery attempt.
The publisher supplies a channel and message payload using the PUBLISH command.
gotchas: A subscriber that is disconnected or cannot process a message loses it permanently; use Pub/Sub only when missing an event is acceptable or another mechanism handles recovery.
Pub/Sub does not retry or replay published messages, so it is unsuitable as the sole transport for durable work or state changes.
Messages published while no matching subscriber is active disappear rather than being queued for later consumers.

Atomicity & messaging::Rate limiting.summary: Redis supports fixed-window, sliding-window, and token-bucket rate limiters. Keep the read–decision–update sequence atomic with Lua EVAL so concurrent requests cannot bypass limits or lose updates.
Atomicity & messaging::Rate limiting.explanation: A Redis rate limiter reads request state, decides whether a request fits the policy, and updates that state. Choose fixed windows for simplicity, sliding windows for recent-history precision, or token buckets for controlled bursts; execute the read–decision–update sequence in one Lua EVAL so concurrent requests cannot interfere.

example.title: Atomic fixed-window limiter
example.explanation: This runnable fixed-window example increments one client/window counter and sets its TTL during the first request; the single script makes the state change atomic.

useCases.title: Fixed-window API quotas
useCases.scenario: A simple quota per API key or route needs low memory and automatic cleanup.

useCases.title: Sliding-window protection
useCases.scenario: A high-value endpoint needs accurate recent-request tracking.

useCases.title: Token-bucket burst control
useCases.scenario: Traffic arrives in bursts but must obey a long-term average rate.

interview.question: How does a fixed-window Redis limiter work?
interview.answer: A fixed window counts requests in a discrete interval, usually with one counter key per client and window. Redis can increment the counter and assign expiration so inactive windows clean themselves up.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent a race between incrementing and expiring? Put both operations in one Lua EVAL, or use an equivalent atomic transaction where appropriate.

interview.question: How would you implement a sliding window?
interview.answer: A sliding-window log stores request timestamps, commonly in a sorted set. The limiter removes timestamps outside the recent window, checks the remaining cardinality, and adds the new request when capacity remains.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off? Accuracy improves, but memory grows with the number of timestamps retained for each client.

interview.question: When is a token bucket preferable?
interview.answer: A token bucket stores the current token count and timing information. Tokens refill according to elapsed time up to the bucket capacity; an allowed request consumes one token, and the refill/check/consume sequence must be atomic.
interview.followUp: Why is atomicity essential? Without it, concurrent requests can each observe the same token and overspend the bucket.

keyPoints: Redis can support the three common policies—fixed window, sliding window, and token bucket—within one deployment.
A fixed-window counter uses INCR for the request count and EXPIRE to remove the completed window automatically.
Choose the Redis structure according to the algorithm: strings for counters, sorted sets for timestamp logs, and hashes for bucket fields.
A Lua script makes state inspection, policy evaluation, and mutation one server-side operation.
gotchas: Do not split reading, deciding, and updating across separate commands: concurrent requests can observe identical state and both pass.

Caching patterns::Cache invalidation.summary: Invalidate cache-aside entries after updating the primary store, then let the next read repopulate them. Per-key TTLs provide an additional bound on stale data.
Caching patterns::Cache invalidation.explanation: In a cache-aside flow, reads check Redis first and repopulate a missing entry from the primary source. After changing the primary record, delete the corresponding Redis key instead of trying to update the cached copy; a later read reconstructs it, while a TTL limits the maximum stale period.

example.title: Invalidate a cache-aside entry after a write
example.explanation: Update the primary record first, then delete its cache key. The next read misses Redis, loads the current record, and stores it again with a bounded TTL.

useCases.title: Entity update invalidation
useCases.scenario: A user, product, or order record changes and its cached representation must no longer be served.

useCases.title: Cache-aside repopulation
useCases.scenario: A read-through cache should recover automatically after an explicit deletion.

useCases.title: Client-side cache notifications
useCases.scenario: Applications use Redis client-side caching and need local entries removed after server-side changes.

useCases.title: TTL-based staleness bound
useCases.scenario: A missed or delayed invalidation must not leave stale data indefinitely.

interview.question: How does cache-aside invalidation work on an update?
interview.answer: Write the updated value to the primary store first, then issue DEL for its Redis cache key. The next read misses the cache, fetches the new primary value, and repopulates Redis.
interview.followUp: How can stale data still be bounded if an invalidation is missed? Use a per-entry EX or PX TTL so entries expire after a configured interval.

interview.question: Describe the read path after invalidation.
interview.answer: The application reads Redis on each request and falls back to the primary store on a miss. It then writes the fetched result back to Redis, typically with a TTL.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the cached object represents a changed record? Delete that object’s key rather than rewriting the cached representation.

interview.question: How does Redis client-side caching notify clients?
interview.answer: Client-side caching tracks keys read by a client and sends invalidation messages when those keys change. Clients must remove the corresponding local entries to avoid serving stale data.
interview.followUp: What timing caveat applies? Invalidation is asynchronous, so removal can occur shortly after the write rather than exactly when it happens.

keyPoints: Perform the primary write before deleting the related cache key, so subsequent reads can rebuild the entry from current data.
After deletion, the first cache miss retrieves the authoritative value and can repopulate Redis.
Use GET and SET with an entry-specific expiration to constrain how long stale data can remain available.
Use DEL for direct, application-controlled invalidation when the source record changes.
A client must evict the notified local key to prevent returning an invalid cached value.
gotchas: Do not attempt to keep the cached value synchronized by rewriting it during the update; delete the key after the primary change.

Caching patterns::Cache stampede.sourceTitle: Cache Layer Architecture: A Practical Guide to Speed & Scale
Caching patterns::Cache stampede.summary: A cache stampede occurs when a popular key expires and many requests regenerate it concurrently. Redis caching solutions mitigate this with request coalescing, TTL jitter, or controlled regeneration through queueing.
Caching patterns::Cache stampede.explanation: A stampede occurs when a popular key expires and many readers miss together. Prevent it by letting one caller regenerate the value while concurrent callers wait for the populated key, or by varying expiration times so misses are distributed. Queueing can additionally smooth bursts when regeneration must be rate-limited.

example.title: Add TTL jitter
example.code:
const ttl = 3600 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 601);
await redis.set("product:42", JSON.stringify(product), { EX: ttl });
example.explanation: Store each value with a slightly different expiration so popular entries do not expire simultaneously.

useCases.title: Single-flight regeneration
useCases.scenario: A high-traffic product or profile key expires and many requests arrive together.

useCases.title: Staggered expirations
useCases.scenario: Many related keys have similar lifetimes and tend to expire together.

useCases.title: Queue-based regeneration
useCases.scenario: Database capacity is limited and cache rebuilds arrive in bursts.

interview.question: What is a cache stampede, and how does request coalescing prevent it?
interview.answer: A cache stampede happens when a popular key expires and many concurrent requests query the database to rebuild it. Request coalescing permits one request to load the value while the others wait for the resulting cache entry.
interview.followUp: How can Redis implement coordination atomically? Use a short-lived lock acquired with SET NX, or an EVAL script that combines the required operations atomically.

interview.question: How does TTL jitter help?
interview.answer: TTL jitter adds a small random component to each entry's expiration time. This staggers expirations and reduces synchronized cache misses across keys.
interview.followUp: When would jitter be insufficient? If one very hot key expires, jitter does not prevent its readers from colliding; combine it with single-flight regeneration.

interview.question: When should controlled regeneration use queueing?
interview.answer: Queueing places regeneration requests into a queue or Redis Streams instead of sending them directly to the database. A worker then processes them at a rate the database can sustain, smoothing bursts.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does queueing introduce? It protects the database but may increase freshness or response latency unless stale values or asynchronous refresh are acceptable.

keyPoints: The failure pattern is synchronized expiration followed by duplicate backend regeneration for the same popular key.
Request coalescing turns concurrent misses into one backend fetch and waiting readers.
TTL jitter spreads expiration events and lowers the chance of a broad synchronized miss.
gotchas: TTL selection trades freshness against cache-hit rate and load: shorter values increase primary traffic, while longer values allow more stale reads.
Treat TTL as the maximum stale-data window, not merely as an eviction preference.

Caching patterns::Cache-aside.summary: Cache-aside checks Redis first, loads the source of truth on a miss, and stores the result with a TTL. Writes update the primary and invalidate the corresponding Redis key.
Caching patterns::Cache-aside.explanation: The application checks Redis for a key on every read. A hit returns immediately; a miss loads the source of truth, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it. On updates, write the primary first and delete the cache key so a later read repopulates it.
Caching patterns::Cache-aside.returns: On a hit, the cached value; on a miss, the value loaded from the primary and then cached.

example.title: Cache-aside read and invalidation
example.explanation: The read path checks Redis, loads the primary store on a miss, and caches the result with a TTL. The write path updates the source of truth first, then removes the cached key.

useCases.title: Read-heavy workloads
useCases.scenario: Repeated reads of popular records can be served from Redis while reducing primary-database traffic.

useCases.title: Working-set caching
useCases.scenario: Only requested entities enter Redis, keeping the cache focused on the active working set.

useCases.title: Bounded-staleness data
useCases.scenario: TTL-based expiration plus write invalidation provides a bounded window for stale data.

interview.question: How does cache-aside work?
interview.answer: The application owns both cache and primary-store access. It checks Redis first, reads the primary on a miss, writes the result to Redis, and returns it.
interview.followUp: What bounds staleness? A per-entry TTL limits how long an uninvalidated value can remain available; explicit deletion handles writes that require fresher reads.

interview.question: What happens on a cache miss?
interview.answer: A cache hit avoids the primary read. A miss loads the source data, stores it under a derived key, commonly with a TTL, and then returns it.
interview.followUp: Why derive keys from request parameters? Equivalent requests must map to the same key so repeated reads can reuse the cached result.

interview.question: How should writes handle cached values?
interview.answer: Update the primary data first, then delete the corresponding Redis key. The next read misses and repopulates Redis from the updated source value.
interview.followUp: What if another process changes the primary? Cache-aside cannot detect that change immediately, so TTL expiration or coordinated invalidation is needed.

keyPoints: Populate Redis only after a requested item misses, rather than preloading all source data.
A hit serves the cached value directly and avoids a primary-database read.
Build deterministic keys from the request inputs so identical queries address the same cached result.
Use an entity-and-identifier key convention and attach a TTL to bound stale-serving time.
The write sequence is primary update followed by cache invalidation.
Lazy population naturally limits Redis contents to data that clients actually request.

Caching patterns::Hot keys and large val.sourceTitle: Redis Enterprise Software observability and monitoring guidance
Caching patterns::Hot keys and large val.summary: Find hot keys and oversized keys before scaling Redis. Hot keys overload one shard, while large values increase CPU and network costs; inspect them with Redis CLI analyzers and then reduce concentration or payload size.
Caching patterns::Hot keys and large val.explanation: A hot key concentrates requests on the single shard that owns it, so that shard can become CPU-bound while other shards remain underused. Large keys—typically hundreds of kilobytes or more—can raise network traffic and CPU usage. Detect both with Redis CLI analysis, then reduce pressure through local caching, splitting data, bounded reads, or asynchronous deletion.

example.title: Inspect hot and large keys
example.code:
redis-cli --hotkeys
redis-cli --memkeys
redis-cli --bigkeys
example.explanation: Run these analyzers against a Redis database to sample frequently accessed keys and inspect memory-heavy keys. Use the findings to decide whether to cache reads locally, split large values, or constrain range queries before adding capacity.

useCases.title: Add an application-local cache for hot reads
useCases.scenario: Read-heavy traffic repeatedly targets one key.

useCases.title: Split an oversized value into smaller keys
useCases.scenario: One collection or payload consumes substantial memory and bandwidth.

useCases.title: Use bounded range reads instead of full scans
useCases.scenario: A sorted set or similar collection is expensive to scan.

useCases.title: Delete asynchronously with UNLINK
useCases.scenario: A huge key must be removed in production.

interview.question: Why can one hot key hurt a Redis cluster even when the cluster has spare capacity?
interview.answer: A hot key is accessed extremely frequently, and Redis places each key on only one shard. Consequently, that shard can experience high CPU utilization and increased latency for unrelated operations. Detect it with hot-key analysis, then consider an application-local cache for read-only traffic.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a hot key that must support writes? Replicate or distribute the data across multiple keys or shards, then reconcile writes at the application layer; local caching alone cannot safely absorb writes.

interview.question: What makes a Redis key 'large,' and how do you find one?
interview.answer: Large keys are values or collections that are hundreds of kilobytes or larger. They can increase network traffic and CPU utilization, so inspect the keyspace with --memkeys or --bigkeys before scaling the cluster.
interview.followUp: What is a safer alternative to repeatedly scanning a large sorted set? Read bounded ranges rather than requesting the complete range from 0 through -1.

interview.question: Which Redis CLI tools help diagnose hot and oversized keys?
interview.answer: Use --hotkeys to sample frequently accessed keys and --memkeys to identify the largest keys and average sizes by type. For --hotkeys, first configure an LFU eviction policy and ensure enough memory is available for eviction.
interview.followUp: What should happen after discovery? Split oversized data, bound range operations, cache read-only hot data locally, and use UNLINK when removing huge keys.

keyPoints: A key cannot spread its workload across shards automatically; all of its requests target the shard that owns it.
A hot key can degrade latency for unrelated requests handled by the same overloaded shard.
Treat values or collections at roughly hundreds of kilobytes and above as candidates for large-key investigation.
Oversized payloads consume more network bandwidth and processing time, making them a capacity and latency concern.
After enabling LFU eviction, use this CLI analyzer to sample keys with unusually high access activity.
Use memkeys to sample the live keyspace and locate memory-heavy keys.
Decompose oversized collections or payloads into smaller keys when one key becomes a bottleneck.

Use UNLINK for very large-key deletion to avoid blocking the server with synchronous DEL.

Caching patterns::TTL and expiration.explanation: A key can have a time-to-live set with EXPIRE or a relative expiration option on a write. Redis automatically deletes the key when its timeout elapses; TTL reports the remaining lifetime. This expiration lifecycle is distinct from eviction, which removes keys to satisfy a database memory limit according to its configured policy.

After the TTL elapses, Redis automatically removes the key.
EXPIRE assigns a relative lifetime to an existing key.

A key without an expiration remains indefinitely unless the application deletes it or another operation changes its lifetime.

Caching patterns::Write-behind tradeoffs.sourceTitle: The complete guide to cache optimization strategies for developers
Caching patterns::Write-behind tradeoffs.summary: Write-behind stores updates in Redis first and persists them to the backing database asynchronously. It lowers write latency and enables batching, but accepts delayed consistency and possible loss of buffered writes if Redis fails or evicts them.
Caching patterns::Write-behind tradeoffs.explanation: Write-behind places the initial write in Redis and propagates it to the backing database asynchronously, often after a delay or in batches. This lowers write latency and can reduce database work, but the interval before persistence creates consistency and durability risks if Redis fails or evicts the buffered data.

example.title: Buffer an update in Redis
example.explanation: The application acknowledges a profile update in Redis first; a separate write-behind component would later flush the changed data to the backing database.

useCases.title: Write-heavy workloads
useCases.scenario: High-volume updates where lower request latency matters more than immediate database persistence.

useCases.title: Batch-friendly changes
useCases.scenario: Multiple updates can be combined before persistence to reduce backend write overhead.

useCases.title: Tolerant business data
useCases.scenario: Data can tolerate a temporary persistence gap and a bounded loss window.

interview.question: What is write-behind caching, and why use it?
interview.answer: Write-behind sends the application’s write to the cache first, then asynchronously forwards it to the database after a delay. Its main benefits are lower write latency and the possibility of batching writes for efficiency.
interview.followUp: What failure must the design tolerate? A cache crash or eviction before the flush can lose buffered writes, so critical data needs a stronger durability strategy.

interview.question: How does write-behind improve write performance?
interview.answer: The cache acknowledges the update immediately, while a background process later propagates it to the backing database. This decouples request latency from persistent-storage latency and can reduce the number of database operations through batching.
interview.followUp: What read behavior follows? Reads may observe data that has not reached the database yet, so consumers must accept eventual consistency or use another coordination mechanism.

interview.question: What are the principal risks?
interview.answer: The central tradeoff is speed and batching efficiency versus consistency and durability. If the cache holding new writes crashes or is evicted before persistence, those writes are lost.
interview.followUp: When is it appropriate? It best fits workloads where delayed persistence and a bounded loss window are acceptable; it is risky for irreplaceable, immediately durable records.

keyPoints: The application’s first write targets Redis rather than the backing database.
A cache-side background process later persists the buffered change.
Write-behind can make requests faster and combine multiple updates before database persistence.
Persistence happens outside the request’s synchronous write path.
gotchas: Buffered updates can be lost when Redis fails or evicts them before the asynchronous database write completes.
Treat write-behind as an eventual-consistency pattern with an explicit data-loss window, not as immediate durable persistence.
A successful cache response does not prove that the backing database already contains the update.

Caching patterns::Write-through caching.summary: Write-through caching places Redis between the application and database: each write updates the cache synchronously and flows to the database. It favors cache–database consistency, but requires handling partial failures and the extra latency of writing to two systems.
Caching patterns::Write-through caching.explanation: The application sends writes through Redis rather than updating the database independently. Redis updates its cached value synchronously and then forwards the change to the database, so successful operations keep both stores aligned; because the operation spans two systems, failure handling must define how to compensate or reconcile a partial write.

example.title: Write through Redis and compensate on database failure
example.explanation: The cache receives the write first, then synchronously persists it to the database; a database failure removes the cache entry to avoid retaining an uncommitted value.

useCases.title: Fresh read models
useCases.scenario: Read-heavy applications with frequently changing records where reads should reflect the latest successful writes.

useCases.title: Staleness-sensitive data
useCases.scenario: Financial data, balances, or inventory counts where stale cached values can cause incorrect decisions.

useCases.title: Consistency over write speed
useCases.scenario: Applications that can tolerate higher write latency in exchange for faster, current reads.

interview.question: How does write-through caching work?
interview.answer: In write-through caching, the cache sits between the application and the operational data store. Updates reach the cache synchronously, and the cache forwards them to the database, favoring consistency between the two stores.
interview.followUp: What happens if only one write succeeds? A partial failure can create inconsistency, so the design must define compensation or reconciliation.

interview.question: What are the primary benefits and costs?
interview.answer: The main benefit is that the cache is updated as part of each write, making newly written data available immediately and reducing the chance of stale cached values. The trade-off is additional write latency because the operation involves both systems.
interview.followUp: When is that trade-off worthwhile? It suits read-heavy workloads where stale data is unacceptable, such as financial or inventory information.

interview.question: What operational pitfalls should be considered?
interview.answer: Write-through can leave cold data in the cache because every write is cached regardless of whether the value will be read. It can also suffer a partial failure between cache and database, which requires explicit recovery handling.
interview.followUp: How could recovery be implemented? Use compensation, retry or reconciliation logic, and define which store is authoritative for repair.

keyPoints: The cache acts as the intermediary on the write path instead of letting the application update the database directly.
A write updates Redis synchronously and then propagates through it to the backing database.
The pattern is chosen primarily to keep cached and durable values aligned.

Client hooks & events::Client error even.summary: Node-Redis emits client errors through the `error` event. Register a listener immediately after creating the client to prevent an unhandled error from unexpectedly terminating the Node.js process.
Client hooks & events::Client error even.explanation: Node-Redis emits an `error` event whenever an error occurs inside the client. Register at least one listener immediately after creating the client, before connecting or issuing commands, so the error is handled rather than propagated as an unhandled EventEmitter error that can terminate the Node.js process.

parameters.name: error
parameters.description: The error object emitted when a client error occurs.

example.title: Register a Redis client error listener
example.explanation: Create the client, register an error listener before connecting, then use and close the connection.

useCases.title: Monitor transport and socket failures
useCases.scenario: Long-running service

interview.question: When should an application attach the Redis client error listener?
interview.answer: Node-Redis emits `error` when an error occurs within the client. Register a listener on the client immediately after `createClient()` so errors are handled and do not become unhandled EventEmitter errors.
interview.followUp: What can happen if the listener is omitted? The system throws the client error, potentially causing the Node.js process to exit unexpectedly.

interview.question: What does the `error` event communicate?
interview.answer: The listener receives the error object as its argument, so the handler can log it or route it to application monitoring. The event commonly represents a network problem, such as an unexpectedly closed socket.
interview.followUp: How should the handler be improved in production? Preserve the error context in structured logs and combine it with the client’s reconnect behavior and application-level recovery policy.

interview.question: Show the basic declaration for an error listener.
interview.answer: Use `client.on('error', handler)` after creating the client and before `connect()`. The listener is a client-level safety requirement, not merely a handler for command results.
interview.followUp: Does the listener replace command-level error handling? No; command failures and recovery decisions still need handling appropriate to the operation, while this listener prevents unhandled client errors.

keyPoints: The client exposes several lifecycle events, but `error` is the critical one for preventing unhandled client failures.
An `error` event is emitted whenever an error occurs inside the Redis client.
Every client should have an error listener as part of its initialization.
Attach the handler with the client’s EventEmitter-style `on` method and the `error` event name.
The handler can record the received error, including a clear Redis-client label and the original error object.
gotchas: A client without at least one error listener can cause the system to throw the error and may unexpectedly exit the Node.js process.

Client hooks & events::Client-side cache.summary: CLIENT TRACKING enables server-assisted client-side caching. Redis remembers keys read by a connection and sends invalidations when those keys change or are evicted, allowing the local cache to drop stale entries.
Client hooks & events::Client-side cache.explanation: With tracking enabled, Redis records keys read by the connection. If a tracked key changes—or is evicted—Redis sends an invalidation message over the same RESP3 connection, or through a redirected connection; the client must remove that key locally to prevent stale results. Broadcasting instead watches configured prefixes without recording individual reads.
Client hooks & events::Client-side cache.syntax: CLIENT TRACKING <ON | OFF> [REDIRECT client-id] [PREFIX prefix [PREFIX prefix ...]] [BCAST] [OPTIN] [OPTOUT] [NOLOOP]

parameters.name: ON | OFF
parameters.description: Enable or disable tracking for the connection.

parameters.name: REDIRECT client-id
parameters.description: Send invalidations to another connection identified by its client ID.

parameters.name: PREFIX prefix [PREFIX prefix ...]
parameters.description: Track or broadcast keys beginning with one or more prefixes.

parameters.name: BCAST
parameters.description: Enable prefix-based broadcasting mode.

parameters.name: OPTIN
parameters.description: Track only explicitly opted-in commands.

parameters.name: OPTOUT
parameters.description: Track commands by default unless explicitly opted out.

parameters.name: NOLOOP
parameters.description: Do not send invalidations for keys modified by this connection.

Client hooks & events::Client-side cache.returns: OK when tracking is successfully enabled or disabled.

example.explanation: Connect with a RESP3-capable client, enable tracking, and read a key; later changes to that key produce an invalidation that the client must use to remove its local copy.

useCases.scenario: A service keeps frequently read Redis objects in process memory and needs changes made by other clients to invalidate those entries.

useCases.title: Use same-connection invalidations
useCases.scenario: A RESP3 client wants invalidations alongside ordinary commands without maintaining a second message connection.

useCases.title: Invalidate by key prefix
useCases.scenario: Applications cache groups of keys and can invalidate them by namespace rather than tracking every read.

useCases.title: Opt in selected cacheable reads

interview.question: What problem does CLIENT TRACKING solve?
interview.answer: CLIENT TRACKING makes Redis remember keys read by a connection. When a remembered key is modified, Redis sends an invalidation message so the client can remove its local copy.
interview.followUp: How can tracking avoid per-key server memory? Use broadcasting mode: subscribe to prefixes and receive notifications for matching keys, without Redis remembering each client's accessed keys.

interview.question: How are invalidation messages delivered?
interview.answer: RESP3 delivers invalidation messages on the tracking connection. RESP2 can use a different connection through redirection, and Pub/Sub is also available for the redirected path.
interview.followUp: Why might a client redirect messages? It separates invalidations from ordinary request and response traffic, which can simplify client-side cache handling.

interview.question: Compare default and broadcasting tracking modes.
interview.answer: Default tracking records keys requested by the client, so notifications are limited to keys that client may have cached. Broadcasting does not track individual reads and instead notifies subscribers when matching prefixes are touched.
interview.followUp: When is broadcasting preferable? It can be useful when prefix-based coverage is acceptable and avoiding server-side per-client tracking memory matters.

keyPoints: CLIENT TRACKING turns on server-assisted client-side caching support for the connection.
Default tracking builds a per-connection record from keys read during the connection lifetime.
A modification to a tracked key triggers an invalidation notification.
Eviction caused by a maxmemory policy is another invalidation trigger.
Broadcasting lets clients receive prefix-based notifications without first requesting each individual key.
gotchas: Same-connection invalidations require RESP3; RESP2 clients need a redirected connection using the available redirection mechanism.
NOLOOP suppresses the notification for a client's own modification, but the tracked key is still removed from the invalidation table.
Receiving a notification is not enough: the client must actually evict the corresponding local entry.

Client hooks & events::Connection lifecy.summary: node-redis emits connect, ready, reconnecting, and end as connection lifecycle events. Use them with isReady and isOpen to distinguish connection progress, command readiness, recovery, and intentional shutdown.
Client hooks & events::Connection lifecy.explanation: A node-redis client emits lifecycle events as it begins connecting, becomes usable, retries after an error, and is intentionally closed. Register listeners on the client to update pool-health state; use isReady for command readiness and isOpen for socket status. Handle error separately because connection failures are reported there.
Client hooks & events::Connection lifecy.returns: The lifecycle events carry no parameters except error, which receives an Error object; client.isReady returns a Boolean.

example.title: Observe node-redis connection events
example.explanation: Registers the documented lifecycle listeners, checks readiness, and intentionally closes the client.

useCases.title: Pool health state
useCases.scenario: A connection pool needs to expose whether a client can currently execute Redis commands.

useCases.title: Connection telemetry
useCases.scenario: An application needs operational visibility into connection attempts and retry cycles.

useCases.title: Graceful shutdown tracking
useCases.scenario: A service must separate planned shutdown from network failure.

interview.question: What do connect and ready mean?
interview.answer: connect means the client is about to begin connecting. ready means the connection has completed and the client can be used; both events carry no parameters.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish socket availability from command readiness? Use isOpen for the underlying socket and isReady for readiness to send commands.

interview.question: When does reconnecting occur?
interview.answer: reconnecting is emitted before node-redis tries to reconnect after an error-related connection loss. Automatic reconnection is enabled by default and can be customized with socket.reconnectionStrategy.
interview.followUp: What behavior should a health check expose during this event? Mark the client as recovering until ready is emitted again, rather than treating the open socket flag alone as sufficient.

interview.question: How should a pool interpret end?
interview.answer: end indicates that the client was intentionally closed with client.quit(). The event has no parameters, so consumers should use it to record planned shutdown rather than infer an unexpected network failure.
interview.followUp: Which event should capture an unexpected connection problem? Listen for error; the documentation describes it as the event carrying the Error parameter.

keyPoints: node-redis exposes connection lifecycle events directly on the client object.
connect marks the beginning of a connection attempt and supplies no event argument.
ready is the event a pool can use to mark a client usable for Redis commands.
reconnecting signals a retry phase after an error-related connection loss.
Use isReady as the direct readiness check when deciding whether the client can send commands.
isOpen reports transport-level socket state, which is distinct from command readiness.
gotchas: Register an error listener as well: connection failures commonly surface as network errors, and an unhandled error can terminate the Node.js process.
Treat reconnecting as recovery activity after an error, not as proof that commands are currently ready to run.
Do not classify every end event as an outage; the documented event represents an intentional quit.

Client hooks & events::Keyspace notifica.summary: Keyspace notifications let Redis clients receive Pub/Sub events for key changes such as expiration and eviction. Use keyspace channels to watch a key, or keyevent channels to watch an operation across keys; notifications are disabled until configured.
Client hooks & events::Keyspace notifica.explanation: Redis publishes notifications through Pub/Sub channels when operations affect the data set. A keyspace channel is organized by key and carries the event name; a keyevent channel is organized by event and carries the key name. Notifications are disabled by default and are enabled with the notify-keyspace-events configuration setting. Expiration and eviction events can then be consumed without repeatedly scanning for missing keys.

example.title: Observe a key expiration
example.explanation: Enables key-event notifications, subscribes to database 0 events, and prints the expired key.

useCases.title: React to cache disappearance
useCases.scenario: A cache-maintenance worker removes related entries when a cached key expires or is evicted.

useCases.title: Track data-set activity
useCases.scenario: An observability consumer counts operations such as expirations or deletions by subscribing to an event pattern.

useCases.title: Monitor one key
useCases.scenario: A service watches changes to a particular key without repeatedly checking its existence.

interview.question: How do keyspace and keyevent notifications differ?
interview.answer: Redis exposes two Pub/Sub channel forms. A keyspace notification uses a channel such as __keyspace@0__:mykey and publishes the event name, while a keyevent notification uses __keyevent@0__:del and publishes the key name.
interview.followUp: Which form is better for monitoring every expiration? Subscribe to the keyevent pattern __keyevent@0__:expired, because the event is fixed and each message identifies the affected key.

interview.question: How are notifications enabled?
interview.answer: Set notify-keyspace-events to a mask containing K for keyspace channels or E for keyevent channels, plus the event-category flags needed by the application. CONFIG SET can change the setting at runtime, and an empty value disables notifications.
interview.followUp: What is the operational trade-off? Notifications consume CPU, so enable only the channel and event categories required by the consumer.

interview.question: Can a consumer rely on notifications for guaranteed delivery?
interview.answer: Notifications use Redis Pub/Sub, which is fire-and-forget. A subscriber that disconnects misses events generated during the gap; Redis does not provide a notification history through this mechanism.
interview.followUp: How can an application recover reliably? Combine notifications with a durable source of truth or periodic reconciliation, rather than treating the event stream as a complete log.

keyPoints: They provide push-based observation of data-set changes, avoiding polling for keys that disappeared.
Expiry events can be scoped to a database, such as database 0.
Redis offers two notification families for each qualifying operation: keyspace and keyevent.
Keyspace channels identify the key in the channel; keyevent channels identify the operation in the channel.
The K configuration flag enables keyspace-channel notifications.
The E configuration flag enables keyevent-channel notifications.
An empty notify-keyspace-events value turns the feature off.
gotchas: Pub/Sub does not replay missed notifications, so a disconnected consumer loses events.
In a cluster, subscribe to every node whose events you need because notifications are node-specific.
Enable notifications deliberately: they add CPU overhead and start disabled.

Client hooks & events::Pub/Sub message h.summary: Pub/Sub handlers run on a dedicated subscriber connection because a subscribed Redis connection cannot handle ordinary commands. With node-redis, duplicate the client and pass a callback to subscribe or pSubscribe.
Client hooks & events::Pub/Sub message h.explanation: A Redis connection that subscribes enters subscribe-only mode, so its message callback must be registered on a dedicated connection. Duplicate the normal client, connect the duplicate, and pass a listener to subscribe; keep the original client for publishing or ordinary commands.
Client hooks & events::Pub/Sub message h.syntax:
await subscriber.subscribe(channel, listener)
await subscriber.pSubscribe(pattern, listener)

example.title: Dedicated subscriber with a message callback
example.explanation: A duplicated connection receives messages through the callback while the original connection remains available for publishing or other Redis commands.

useCases.scenario: Invalidate application cache entries when another process publishes a change notification.

useCases.title: Worker event processing
useCases.scenario: Deliver notifications to workers that subscribe to exact event channels.

useCases.title: Pattern-based routing
useCases.scenario: Listen to a family of channels such as cache:invalidate:* without registering each channel individually.

interview.question: Why should a Pub/Sub subscriber use a separate Redis connection?
interview.answer: A subscriber connection enters a restricted mode after subscribing, so it should not be used for normal commands. The client documentation recommends creating a dedicated connection for the subscription.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve access to ordinary commands? Duplicate the main client, connect the duplicate, and use that duplicate only for subscriptions.

interview.question: How is a message handler wired in node-redis?
interview.answer: With node-redis, register the callback as the second argument to subscribe. The callback receives each published message for the subscribed channel.
interview.followUp: How would you handle several channels? Subscribe to each required channel, or use pattern subscriptions when channel names follow a pattern.

interview.question: When would you choose SUBSCRIBE versus PSUBSCRIBE?
interview.answer: SUBSCRIBE adds exact channel subscriptions, while PSUBSCRIBE matches channel-name patterns. Redis delivers published messages to currently subscribed clients in publication order.
interview.followUp: What trade-off comes with pattern subscriptions? They can cover a channel hierarchy without registering every channel, but broad patterns may receive more messages than needed.

keyPoints: After subscription, Redis pushes matching messages through the same socket rather than treating the connection like a normal command client.
Use a duplicate client to isolate the subscribe-mode connection from the client used for ordinary application work.
The handler is supplied directly to subscribe for exact channels or pSubscribe for patterns.
Handlers observe messages in publication order for the messages delivered to the subscriber.
Publishing sends the payload to every currently subscribed client for the selected channel.
gotchas: Do not use the subscribed connection for ordinary Redis operations; retain a separate connection for them.
Subscription management remains possible on the subscribed connection, but ordinary command execution does not.

Client hooks & events::Reconnect strateg.summary: Configure node-redis reconnection with a fixed delay, disablement, or a custom function. A bounded exponential delay plus random jitter prevents synchronized clients from repeatedly hitting a failing server.
Client hooks & events::Reconnect strateg.explanation: When node-redis loses its connection, it can call a user-supplied reconnect strategy with the retry count. The function returns a delay in milliseconds for the next attempt; adding jitter and a maximum cap spreads retries across clients and limits how aggressively a failing server is contacted. Returning false disables reconnection, while a number supplies a fixed delay.

parameters.name: retries

interview.question: How do you configure a custom reconnect strategy in node-redis?
interview.answer: Set `socket.reconnectStrategy` to a function. It receives the retry count and returns the delay before the next attempt; it can also determine how reconnection is handled.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid a retry storm? Use exponential growth, cap the delay, and add random jitter so clients do not retry in sync.

interview.question: What configuration choices are available for reconnection?
interview.answer: The strategy can be disabled with `false`, use a fixed millisecond delay with a number, or compute behavior dynamically with a function. The default behavior is automatic exponential backoff with jitter.
interview.followUp: When might a fixed delay be preferable? In a tightly controlled environment with a small client population and predictable recovery timing, though it provides less coordination resistance.

interview.question: How should a reconnect delay function be designed?
interview.answer: A practical function calculates an exponential delay such as [2m[2m2 to the power of retries[0m multiplied by a base interval, limits it to a maximum, then adds random jitter. This bounds server load while allowing progressively longer recovery attempts.
interview.followUp: Why cap the delay? Without a cap, later retries can become unnecessarily slow; the cap defines the maximum recovery interval.

keyPoints: Automatic reconnection is available after the client loses its server connection.
Configure reconnection behavior inside the client's socket options.
A numeric strategy creates a constant delay, expressed in milliseconds.
A function lets the application calculate retry behavior rather than using one fixed interval.
Random jitter can be added to separate otherwise synchronized client attempts.
The documented pattern combines exponential growth with a 3-second maximum delay.
gotchas: The documented option is named `reconnectStrategy` in the client configuration example; use the exact current API spelling.
Replacing the default strategy removes its built-in jitter, so add equivalent randomization if many clients may reconnect together.
Returning or configuring a disabling value prevents automatic recovery; choose this only when reconnection is handled elsewhere.

Client hooks & events::Server-side scrip.summary: Run Lua scripts or Redis Functions on the server to make multi-step reads and writes atomic. This prevents clients from interleaving commands during a read-modify-write operation.
Client hooks & events::Server-side scrip.explanation: A Lua script or Redis function executes the read, decision, and write on the Redis server as one atomic operation. Redis blocks other server activity while it runs, so another client cannot interleave commands into the middle of the sequence. Use KEYS for key names and ARGV for other inputs.

parameters.description: Lua source code to execute, or the registered function name for FCALL.

parameters.name: numkeys and keys

parameters.name: args

useCases.scenario: A counter, quota, or token-bucket update must inspect current state before writing a new value.

useCases.title: Cross-key consistency
useCases.scenario: One logical operation must update related values stored under multiple keys.

useCases.title: Server-side multi-step workflows
useCases.scenario: Application logic would otherwise require several client-server round trips.

interview.question: Why can a server-side script prevent a read-modify-write race?
interview.answer: Redis executes a script atomically on the server, and its effects appear as though they all happened or none had happened. The execution blocks other server activity, preventing another client from interleaving the read and write.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off of this guarantee? A long-running script delays every connected client until it finishes.

interview.question: How does a Lua script interact with Redis data?
interview.answer: A Lua script invokes Redis commands with redis.call() or redis.pcall(). The script receives key names through KEYS and other values through ARGV, allowing the complete operation to remain server-side.
interview.followUp: When should pcall be preferred? Use it when a Redis command error should be returned to the script instead of immediately aborting it.

interview.question: How do Redis Functions differ from ad hoc Lua scripts?
interview.answer: Redis Functions provide server-managed code that is declared before invocation and called by name with FCALL. They retain atomic execution while avoiding the need to send or reload script source for every call.
interview.followUp: What is a function-specific safety option? A no-writes flag can identify read-only functions so Redis can run them with read-only safeguards.

keyPoints: Lua scripts move application logic into Redis, reducing client-server round trips for multi-step operations.
The entire script is indivisible from other clients' perspective.
A client observes the script before it has taken effect or after its complete effect, not a partial state.
One script can inspect conditions and update several keys as a single operation.
Use redis.call for normal command execution or redis.pcall when command errors should be handled by the script.
For Redis 7+, Functions are the durable, named server-side programmability option.
gotchas: Long-running scripts or functions pause every connected client, so keep server-side logic short.
Read-only script variants cannot perform updates; use a regular execution command when the hook writes data.

Learning module::Redis learning module.summary: Redis is an open-source, in-memory key-value data structure store. It can serve as a cache, database, message broker, streaming engine, document store, and vector search platform.
Learning module::Redis learning module.explanation: Redis keeps key-value data in memory and maps each unique key to a typed value. Applications can use its data structures for fast caching, persistence-backed storage, messaging, and event streaming.

interview.question: What is Redis?
interview.answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value data structure store. A unique key maps to a typed value, and supported values include strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, JSON, and vector sets.
interview.followUp: How does Redis support document storage? Store JSON documents and query them with Redis's JSON capabilities rather than modeling every field as a separate key.

interview.question: Why is Redis useful for caching and messaging?
interview.answer: Redis is commonly used as a cache because its in-memory design provides very fast reads and writes. Applications can also use it as a database, message broker, and streaming engine.
interview.followUp: When would Streams be preferable to Pub/Sub? Use Streams when durable, consumer-group-based processing is required; Pub/Sub is intended for real-time channel delivery.

interview.question: How does Redis support vector workloads?
interview.answer: Redis supports vector search through vector sets and indexed vector fields in Hash or JSON documents. This lets applications store embeddings with associated metadata and query them semantically.
interview.followUp: How can Redis support both structured and semantic retrieval? Keep metadata in Hash or JSON fields, index vectors alongside it, and combine vector queries with metadata filtering.

keyPoints: One Redis deployment can cover caching, database storage, message brokering, and stream processing.
Redis uses a NoSQL key-value model rather than requiring relational tables.
Keys identify values, while the value type determines which operations are available.
Choose the native structure that matches the access pattern, such as Lists for sequences or Sorted Sets for ranked members.
Publishers write to channels and subscribers receive messages without direct service-to-service coupling.
Streams provide a persistence-oriented messaging model with consumer groups for coordinated processing.
gotchas: Memory-first operation provides speed, but applications should account for memory capacity and configure persistence when data must survive restarts.
Pub/Sub is real-time messaging; Redis Streams are the better fit when messages need persistence and consumer groups.

Redis foundations::Hashes.summary: Redis hashes group an entity's named fields under one key. They support field-level reads, writes, and counter updates, avoiding replacement of one serialized object for every small change.
Redis foundations::Hashes.explanation: A Redis hash stores an entity as a Redis key containing multiple field-value pairs. Commands can read or change one field without serializing and replacing the entire entity, while numeric fields can be updated with counter commands.
Redis foundations::Hashes.syntax:
HSET key field value [field value ...]
HGET key field
HGETALL key
HINCRBY key field increment

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Redis key identifying the hash

parameters.name: field/value
parameters.description: One or more field names and their values for HSET; a field name for HGET

Redis foundations::Hashes.returns: HGET returns a field value; HGETALL returns all field-value pairs; HSET creates or modifies fields.

example.title: Store and update user fields
example.code:
HSET user:1001 name "Ada" plan "pro" login_count 3
HGET user:1001 plan
HINCRBY user:1001 login_count 1
HGETALL user:1001
example.explanation: This creates a user record, reads one field, atomically increments a numeric field, and retrieves the complete hash.

useCases.title: Basic objects
useCases.scenario: Store profile, configuration, or device attributes as separate named values.

useCases.title: Grouped counters
useCases.scenario: Keep related integer metrics under one entity key and update them independently.

useCases.title: Partial cache updates
useCases.scenario: Change one cached attribute without encoding and rewriting the whole record.

interview.question: What is a Redis hash, and why use one for an object?
interview.answer: A hash is a record-like collection of field-value pairs stored under one Redis key. It is useful for basic objects and grouped counters, and lets applications update individual fields rather than replacing one serialized value.
interview.followUp: When would HGETALL be inappropriate? For a large hash, retrieve only required fields with HGET or HMGET to avoid returning every field.

interview.question: How do the main hash access commands differ?
interview.answer: HSET creates or modifies a field, and HGET reads one field. HGETALL reads the complete hash; the documented complexities are O(1) for HSET and HGET and O(N) for HGETALL.
interview.followUp: How can a client reduce round trips while reading several fields? Use HMGET, which returns values for multiple requested fields.

interview.question: How are counters represented inside a hash?
interview.answer: HINCRBY increments an integer-valued field by a supplied amount. If the field is absent, Redis starts from zero, making the command useful for grouped counters.
interview.followUp: What should be checked before using HINCRBY? The existing value must be interpretable as an integer; otherwise the increment cannot be applied.

keyPoints: A hash models one record as named fields grouped under a single Redis key.
Hashes suit lightweight objects and sets of related counters.
HSET both adds new fields and overwrites values for fields that already exist.
HGET reads one named field without fetching unrelated values.
HGETALL reconstructs the complete field map returned by Redis.
HGETALL scales with the number of fields returned, unlike constant-time single-field access.
gotchas: HGETALL returns every field and value, so retrieving a large hash can cost more than reading selected fields.
HINCRBY treats a missing field as zero; confirm that this default matches the application's intended initialization.

Redis foundations::JSON and search capab.summary: Redis stores searchable documents as hashes or JSON objects and maintains secondary indexes over selected fields. Verify that the deployed Redis environment enables the JSON and search capabilities your application needs.
Redis foundations::JSON and search capab.explanation: Redis keeps documents in hashes or JSON values and maintains separate secondary indexes that reference them. JSON storage supports nested structures through JSONPath, while field types determine whether searches perform text matching, exact tag filtering, numeric ranges, geographic queries, or vector similarity. JSON search requires the relevant JSON and search capabilities to be enabled in the database.
Redis foundations::JSON and search capab.syntax: FT.CREATE index ON JSON PREFIX count prefix SCHEMA field AS alias type ...

example.title: Index and search a JSON document
example.code:
FT.CREATE idx ON JSON PREFIX 1 doc: SCHEMA $.title AS title TEXT $.price AS price NUMERIC
JSON.SET doc:1 $ '{"title":"Redis","price":10}'
FT.SEARCH idx '@title:Redis @price:[0 20]'
example.explanation: Stores a JSON document, creates a secondary index over JSONPath fields, and searches text and numeric values.

useCases.scenario: Applications with hierarchical records

useCases.title: Filter structured fields
useCases.scenario: Exact filters, ranges, or ordering

useCases.title: Run vector similarity search
useCases.scenario: Semantic retrieval over embeddings
